claims.text: The initial conventionally cast WNbMoTa alloy has minimal secondary phases.
Adding approximately 1–2 at.% Ti and a low carbon content, followed by carburization at approximately 1200°C for 1–2 hours and rapid cooling, will form TiC in situ in WNbMoTa.
The intervention will produce a uniform dispersion of TiC precipitates smaller than 50 nm.
An optimized heat treatment and potential minor alloying changes will stabilize the TiC precipitates against coarsening.
Fine TiC precipitates hinder dislocation motion and cause precipitation strengthening.
TiC precipitates act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
Defect absorption by TiC will reduce defect clustering and radiation-induced softening.
The treated alloy will have higher yield strength than conventionally processed WNbMoTa lacking the designed TiC microstructure.
The treated alloy will have greater hardness than conventionally processed WNbMoTa lacking the designed TiC microstructure.
The TiC-containing alloy will show improved resistance to irradiation-induced degradation.
The TiC-containing alloy will maintain high-temperature thermal stability.
The predicted improvements will hold above 850°C.
The predicted improvements will hold at irradiation doses relevant to service environments.
Long-term exposure may cause nanoscale TiC precipitate coarsening and may require further heat-treatment optimization.
A treated group and a conventionally processed control group can be compared using mechanical tests, TEM, and irradiation-defect measurements.
Failure to obtain statistically significant mechanical improvement and reduced irradiation damage relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
